solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Slight wound is no handicap

definitions.meaning: a minor graze or nick on the skin
in golf a player who plays off zero, with no strokes given, is said to play off this

explanation.surface: A minor injury is said not to hold someone back.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf a player with no handicap is called a 'scratch' player.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: a minor skin graze, and the golfing term for a zero handicap.

clue.text: Implement warder's given to cabbie

parts.note: a screw is slang for a prison warder; the 's stands for 'is', a link
a cabbie is a taxi driver

explanation.surface: A prison officer apparently passes some tool on to a taxi driver.
explanation.walkthrough: SCREW is British prison slang for a warder.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool for turning screws is a common workshop implement.

clue.text: Article's condemned singer's performance, say

indicators.note: something condemned is wrecked or ruined, so the letters of the word are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A newspaper article pans a singer's show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'condemned' looks like a review's verdict but signals the anagram of ARTICLE; 'say' marks a singer's show as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A solo concert by a singer is an example of this kind of musical performance.

clue.text: Cheap, at 200 for a pound?

definitions.meaning: costing very little, of little worth
a pound was 240 old pence, now 100 new pence; 200 for a pound is two for each penny, read literally

explanation.surface: A bargain priced at two hundred items per pound.
explanation.walkthrough: With 100 pence in a pound, 200 for a pound is two for every penny, the literal reading of the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom describes something so plentiful that it is worth almost nothing.

clue.text: The village prince

definitions.meaning: a small settlement, smaller than a town
Shakespeare's Prince of Denmark is the title character of his tragedy

explanation.surface: A prince who lives in, or rules, a village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' is just a link joining the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A small rural settlement is one sense; the other is Shakespeare's Danish prince.

clue.text: Confront Bill with fine

parts.note: F is short for fine, as on pencil grades
an ace is American slang for a one-dollar bill

explanation.surface: Someone must stand up to a man named Bill who has been fined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name or an invoice, but here it is the dollar note called an ace.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand up to someone or something head-on is to confront it.

clue.text: Service thrown up a long way

indicators.note: in a down entry, thrown up means the letters run from bottom to top

parts.note: the RAF, Royal Air Force, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A tennis serve tossed high travels a great distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests tennis but means one of the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Something a long way off is distant, a simple synonym.

clue.text: Stupid person caught by sleeping policeman

parts.note: C is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
British slang for a speed bump in the road, a hump

explanation.surface: A fool is arrested by a policeman who was asleep on duty.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'sleeping policeman' is a British term for a road hump, not a dozy officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A chump is an informal word for a fool or idiot.

clue.text: Page in directory

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the word directory

explanation.surface: A page found in a phone directory.
explanation.definitionFit: The right-hand page of an open book is the recto, a printing term.

clue.text: One may be up for a party in the garden

definitions.text: One may be up for a party in the garden

parts.words: One may be up for a party in the garden
parts.note: 'up' suggests a keen guest, but means put up, erected, as a large tent is for a garden party

explanation.surface: Someone keen to attend a garden party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up for' reads as eager, but the thing is literally up, pitched on the lawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A large tent is put up on the lawn for garden parties and weddings.

clue.text: Part of continental breakfast set prized by footballers?

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase standing for the trophy that is prized

parts.note: continental refers to mainland Europe
a breakfast set of crockery includes a cup, the part the clue's opening words point to

explanation.surface: A piece of continental breakfast crockery is treasured by footballers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'continental breakfast' looks like one phrase, but splits into the adjective and the cup from the breakfast set.
explanation.definitionFit: The trophy for Europe's top club football competition is coveted by players.

clue.text: From the start, worker is trading intelligence

indicators.note: from the start of each word, take only its opening letter

explanation.surface: A worker has sold information from day one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intelligence' looks like secret information, but it means cleverness.
explanation.definitionFit: Quickness of mind or mental sharpness is an old sense of the word.

clue.text: Rat-catcher departs by sewer into breakwater

indicators.note: into says the departs-and-sewer pieces go inside the breakwater

parts.note: a pier can act as a barrier against the waves
D is the timetable abbreviation for departs
a sewer is a large drainage pipe

explanation.surface: A rat-catcher leaves through a sewer that leads into a sea wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sewer' could be someone who sews, but here it is a drain.
explanation.definitionFit: In the legend of Hamelin, a piper lured away the town's rats with his music.

clue.text: Horribly abuse pill? Only too credible

indicators.note: horribly suggests a mangling of the words abuse pill into a new order

explanation.surface: A story about pill abuse sounds all too believable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something seemingly reasonable and believable, perhaps deceptively so, fits 'only too credible'.

clue.text: Show mercy, soldiers — fast

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, is a British army corps
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: An appeal to soldiers to be merciful, and quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' looks like 'quickly' but is the noun: the Lenten fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To soften and give way, becoming less harsh, is to relent.

clue.text: Being poor is difficult at university

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase: being short of money

parts.note: hard means difficult
in British usage a student is up at university

explanation.surface: Student poverty is tough.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge means being in residence there.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase describes someone short of money, so in a state of being poor.

clue.text: One's picked up in warehouse. and one's put down

indicators.note: in places the upturned piece within the warehouse

parts.note: a depot is a storehouse

indicators.note: in a down entry, picked up means read upwards

parts.note: I is one, and 's is 'is', giving IS

explanation.surface: Something is collected from a warehouse and something else is dropped off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' sounds like collecting goods, but in a down light it means the letters read upwards; 'One's' is used twice, once in the wordplay and once in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Money or sediment laid down is a deposit, something put down.

clue.text: Believe Devon town's not working

indicators.note: not removes the word for working from the town's name

parts.note: Crediton is a small town in Devon, a county in south-west England
on means working, as a machine that is switched on

explanation.surface: Believe it or not, a Devon town has stopped functioning.
explanation.walkthrough: CREDITON is a market town in Devon, in south-west England; 'not working' drops ON.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept something as true is to believe it, as in 'I can't credit it'.

clue.text: Orchards invaders wrecked over years

indicators.note: over says the scrambled letters lie over and around the abbreviation
wrecked suggests the word invaders smashed into a new order

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year or years

explanation.surface: Invading armies laid waste to orchards over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrecked' turns INVADERS into VINEARDS, and 'over' wraps it round Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Plantations of grapevines are loosely fruit orchards.

clue.text: Sound from hooter enveloping one

indicators.note: enveloping says the hooter wraps round the one

parts.note: hooter is British slang for a nose
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A noise comes from a car horn around one person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hooter' suggests a car horn but is slang for a nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything heard is a sound; this word is a general synonym for it.

clue.text: Veg is not quite fruit

indicators.note: not quite means drop the final letter of the fruit

parts.note: a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: A vegetable is not quite a fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: This small green seed is a common vegetable.

clue.text: Was head of state, but stepped down, not having succeeded

indicators.note: not having says the abbreviation is dropped

parts.note: to resign is to step down from office
S is a genealogy abbreviation for succeeded

explanation.surface: A ruler who quit before achieving anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'succeeded' looks like 'did well' but gives S.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch who ruled held power as head of state.

clue.text: Indicate approval as new party set up

indicators.note: in a down entry, set up means written upwards

parts.note: do is informal for a party

explanation.surface: Someone gives the go-ahead for a new party being organised.
explanation.definitionFit: A dip of the head is a gesture of assent.

clue.text: Not advanced from first degree, that's what I meant

parts.note: a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a first university degree
sic is inserted to say a word is meant exactly as written

explanation.surface: A speaker clarifies that a first degree is not advanced study.
explanation.walkthrough: SIC, Latin for 'thus', marks a quotation as deliberately exact.
explanation.definitionFit: Elementary or fundamental, the opposite of advanced.

clue.text: Not many would be heard in squabble

indicators.note: be heard means the words are spoken and sound like another word

parts.note: not many is few; few would shortens to few'd

explanation.surface: Only a few people would listen to a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not many would' gives FEW'D, which said out loud matches the word for a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A prolonged bitter quarrel is a feud; squabble is a lighter synonym.

clue.text: Where baby rocks the crown?

definitions.meaning: a tree's crown is its upper branches

explanation.surface: A royal infant rocking the crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baby rocks the crown' suggests a royal heir, but it is the nursery rhyme cradle and a tree's canopy.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper branches of a tree are called its crown.
